A customer closes her account, and the app soft-deletes it. A month later she signs up again with the same email and gets a 500:
Cannot insert duplicate key row in object 'dbo.Customers' with unique index 'IX_Customers_Email'
. Meanwhile her orders still count in the sales report but vanish from the order page that shows the customer's name. And the new admin "Trash" page, built with
, lists deleted customers from every tenant, not just the admin's own.
The belief: soft delete is an
column plus a global query filter, and everything else keeps working as before. Deleted rows disappear from queries,
and navigations respect the filter, and nothing else in the app has to know.
That's how EF Core's own documentation introduces query filters: its first example is soft deletion with

, and it really does hide those rows from every LINQ query on that type, including loads through navigations. The half-truth is the word "everything". The filter changes reads. Deleting, constraints and relationships work exactly as they did before, and they still think the row exists.

blocks.title: Opinion: soft delete is a feature, not a default

content.text: This is our view, not a rule from the docs. Soft-delete the entities users actually restore or that you must keep for audit, and hard-delete the rest. Every soft-deleted type carries all of the above, plus data that grows forever.
